description: Hi! I’m Hana, a 9th grader who loves space and astrophysics. I’ve won inter‑school and global competitions, and I enjoy storytelling. Our topic is Abandoned, Not Forgotten, the stories of what NASA left on the Moon and why they matter. No experience needed, just curiosity! We’re looking for people who enjoy astrophysics, storytelling, and creativity.
summary:
There is a car parked on the Moon. It has been there since 1971. Nobody is coming back for it.

That fact surprised me, so I built a website about it. It’s a museum of six machines NASA left behind, and you are the investigator. Each case file opens with a mystery.

Why did no one come back for the car? How did two rovers built for 90 days keep going for years? What cast a flying shadow on Mars? How does a mirror on the Moon still answer us, 57 years later? Who cut open a robot on the Moon, and why? And where is Voyager 1 going?

As you scroll, each story plays out with real NASA photos and the astronauts’ own words. You can fire a laser at the Moon and wait the real 2.5 seconds for the light to come back.

Every case answers one question: when does a tool become history?

The last case is not solved. People are going back to the Moon soon. Should these machines be protected, studied or brought home? On my website, you decide.
details:
My project is a website that works like a museum. It has six machines NASA left behind, and you are the investigator. You scroll, and each case plays out with real NASA photos. Every case starts with a mystery and ends by answering my main question: when does a tool become history?

I made it because most kids my age only hear about missions that are still running. I didn’t even know there was a car on the Moon until I started this. I want students aged 10 to 15 to care about these old machines and the science they did. At the end, you decide what should happen to them, because people are going back to the Moon soon.

My favourite part is the laser button. You fire a laser at the mirror Apollo 11 left behind and wait 2.5 seconds for the light to come back, which is the real time it takes.

I built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The photos and facts come from NASA, mainly the NASA Image and Video Library. I used Claude, an AI assistant, to help check facts, edit the story and write code. Every photo is real.

I checked each fact against NASA sources and kept the sentences short. The site is free and works on phones.
